subject: biology
title: Should laboratory-grown skin be approved for burn treatment?
scenario: Two skin cultures are grown from the same patient. Culture A forms tissue in 12 days but 7% of cells show abnormal division. Culture B takes 18 days, has 1% abnormal cells and survives better after transfer. Both are grown in nutrient solution and monitored using images with scale bars.
finalPrompt: Use the evidence to recommend which culture should be used. Explain how cell structures, membrane transport, mitosis, differentiation and microscopy determine whether the replacement skin will function safely.
finalModelAnswer: Use image size ÷ actual size with consistent units; compare actual cell dimensions and repeated fields of view, not apparent image size. Water enters by osmosis through partially permeable membranes; excessive gain can swell and damage cells, so water potential must be controlled. Surface-area-to-volume ratio falls and diffusion distance rises, so inner cells receive less oxygen/glucose and removal of waste slows. Mitosis supplies genetically identical cells for repair, but loss of cell-cycle control can cause a tumour; Culture A’s higher abnormal fraction increases risk. Cells must differentiate and organise into tissues with specialised structures; a mass of undifferentiated cells may not provide an effective barrier. Patient-derived cells can differentiate and reduce immune rejection, but contamination, mutation and uncontrolled division still require monitoring. Use many independent cultures, standardised conditions, blinded scoring, means and spread, and statistical comparison of abnormal-cell proportions. Culture B is slower but currently safer and more viable; approve only if long-term function, tumour risk and reproducibility are demonstrated.

subject: biology
title: Why did one runner collapse after the same meal and race?
scenario: Two runners eat identical starchy meals. Runner A has normal villi, reaches a blood glucose peak of 7.8 mmol dm⁻³ and completes the race. Runner B has damaged villi, reaches 5.9 mmol dm⁻³, becomes breathless and develops chest pain. Their lung volumes are similar.
finalPrompt: Use the evidence to explain the different outcomes. Connect digestion, enzymes, absorption, gas exchange, blood, heart and vessels, then evaluate which additional test would best identify Runner B’s limiting problem.
requiredPracticalLinks: Food tests; effect of pH on amylase
finalModelAnswer: Amylase hydrolyses starch to soluble sugars; unsuitable pH changes the active site and lowers enzyme-substrate complex formation. Damaged villi reduce surface area and may increase diffusion distance, lowering glucose absorption; Runner B’s smaller rise supports but does not prove this. Exchange also depends on alveolar area, membrane thickness, concentration gradient and perfusion; lung volume alone is insufficient. Glucose is dissolved in plasma; oxygen binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, then both are delivered through capillaries. Restricted coronary arteries reduce oxygen to cardiac muscle, limiting aerobic respiration and causing pain even if ventilation is normal. Arteries have thick elastic muscular walls for high pressure; capillaries have one-cell-thick walls and narrow lumens for rapid exchange. Low glucose supports reduced absorption; chest pain strongly indicates cardiac oxygen shortage; both may contribute and correlation alone is not causal proof. Blood oxygen, ECG/exercise test, coronary imaging and post-meal glucose could separate gas-exchange, cardiac and absorption explanations; select the test that most directly distinguishes them.

subject: biology
title: Which outbreak-control strategy should a school adopt?
scenario: A respiratory illness spreads through a school. Group X has 92% vaccine uptake and 8 cases per 1000 students. Group Y has 54% uptake and 41 cases per 1000. An antibiotic prescription does not change recovery time. A rapid test has 96% sensitivity but 90% specificity.
finalPrompt: Evaluate an outbreak-control plan using the data. Connect pathogen biology, transmission, immune response, vaccination, antibiotics, diagnostic testing and drug trials, and explain the limitations of the evidence.
finalModelAnswer: Antibiotics do not kill viruses, so viral infection is plausible; resistance, wrong drug or non-adherence mean the result alone is not proof. Fewer infectious contacts reduce opportunities for droplets to transmit; interrupted chains mean each prevented case can prevent later cases. Memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen and rapidly produce specific antibodies, often preventing symptoms and onward transmission. The association is strong, but age, behaviour, prior infection and testing could confound; matched groups or adjusted analysis strengthen causality. Imperfect sensitivity gives false negatives who may transmit; imperfect specificity isolates some uninfected students, so confirmatory testing may be needed. Use sterile technique, equal inoculum/discs, controlled concentration and incubation, repeats, and compare clear-zone area or diameter. Randomise, blind, use placebo/standard care, adequate sample size, predefined outcomes and adverse-event monitoring; compare recovery and transmission. Promote vaccination, isolate likely cases, use accurate testing and ventilation; do not use antibiotics routinely; review outcomes while protecting vulnerable people.

subject: biology
title: How should a vertical farm maximise food yield without wasting energy?
scenario: Lettuce is grown under three lamps. At 100, 200 and 400 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹ light, mean growth is 3.2, 5.9 and 6.2 g day⁻¹. Electricity use doubles at each step. At 30 °C growth falls to 4.1 g day⁻¹ although light is unchanged. Nitrate concentration is low.
finalPrompt: Use the evidence to recommend operating conditions. Explain limiting factors, photosynthesis, use of glucose, respiration and biomass, and evaluate the design and economic validity of the investigation.
finalModelAnswer: Light is no longer the main limiting factor; carbon dioxide, temperature, chlorophyll, nitrate or another resource limits the rate. Photosynthetic reactions are enzyme controlled; above the optimum, altered active sites and increased respiration can reduce net biomass gain. Glucose may be respired or converted to cellulose, starch, lipids and amino acids; only retained material contributes to net biomass. Nitrate is required for amino acids/proteins; deficiency restricts growth even when carbon fixation is high. Respiration continues and consumes stored glucose while photosynthesis stops, so carbon dioxide is released and dry biomass can decrease. The 200 treatment nearly doubles growth from 100 but 400 adds little while doubling energy again; calculate yield per energy to support the choice. Use replicates, control temperature/CO₂/water/minerals, randomise positions, measure dry mass, and vary one factor across a suitable range. Use near 200 light units, maintain optimum temperature and correct nitrate/CO₂; verify energy price, crop quality and long-term replicated yield before scaling.

subject: biology
title: Should a runner continue after the monitoring system warns of danger?
scenario: During a hot race, core temperature rises from 37.0 to 39.4 °C, blood glucose falls from 5.2 to 3.4 mmol dm⁻³ and urine output falls. After drinking plain water, body mass remains 1.8% below the starting value. A sensor gives one unusually high reading.
finalPrompt: Evaluate whether the runner should continue. Connect nervous and hormonal coordination, thermoregulation, blood glucose, kidneys, ADH and negative feedback, and judge the reliability and limitations of the monitoring evidence.
finalModelAnswer: Temperature is high, glucose is low and reduced urine suggests water conservation; several interacting deviations increase risk. The brain coordinates vasodilation and sweating, but high humidity reduces evaporation, so less thermal energy is transferred from skin. Electrical impulses through sensory/CNS/motor pathways act rapidly and briefly; hormones travel in blood and usually act more slowly and longer. Glucagon promotes glycogen-to-glucose conversion; finite glycogen stores and high muscle demand may mean blood glucose remains low. More ADH increases collecting-duct permeability, so more water is reabsorbed and a smaller volume of concentrated urine forms. Sweating supports cooling but removes water, increasing osmotic stress and ADH; conserving water cannot replace water already lost. Check calibration and repeat measurement, but do not dismiss it when independent temperature, mass and glucose evidence also indicate danger. Stop, cool, rehydrate appropriately and seek assessment; combined hyperthermia, hypoglycaemia and dehydration outweigh performance benefit despite measurement uncertainty.

subject: biology
title: Should a gene-edited crop be released?
scenario: A gene-edited wheat line yields 18% more during drought and has 35% less fungal disease. In three field sites, a resistance allele appears in 2%, 6% and 19% of nearby wild grass seeds. The edited plants show unchanged protein content, but the trial lasted only two seasons.
finalPrompt: Evaluate whether release should be approved. Connect DNA, genes and proteins, meiosis and variation, inheritance, natural selection, genetic engineering, biodiversity and the strength of the field evidence.
finalModelAnswer: A changed gene may alter amino-acid sequence and protein shape/function, changing the plant’s interaction with the fungus. Meiosis, sexual reproduction, mutations and environmental differences produce variation beyond the edited allele. Gene flow occurred and varies by site; distance, wind and population size may explain variation, so one overall percentage would conceal pattern. Carriers may survive/reproduce more, increasing allele frequency over generations and potentially altering competition. Absolute yield, variation, drought severity, costs and performance in non-drought years are needed to judge practical benefit. Transfer could increase weed fitness, change competition and food webs, and reduce local biodiversity; probability and magnitude both matter. Multiple sites help, but two seasons are too short for rare effects, evolutionary change and varied climates; independent longer trials are needed. Limit release initially, use buffer zones and genetic monitoring, publish independent data, and expand only if benefits persist and gene-flow impacts remain acceptable.

subject: biology
title: How should a damaged river catchment be restored?
scenario: Upstream nitrate rises from 3 to 11 mg dm⁻³ below farmland. Algal cover rises from 18% to 76%, dissolved oxygen falls from 9.1 to 3.8 mg dm⁻³ and mayfly abundance falls by 82%. A proposed wetland would remove an estimated 55% of nitrate but convert 6 hectares of grassland.
finalPrompt: Use the data to design and justify a restoration strategy. Connect abiotic and biotic factors, sampling, decomposition, nutrient cycling, biodiversity, land use and food security, and evaluate trade-offs and uncertainty.
finalModelAnswer: Nitrate increases algal growth; shading kills plants; decomposers respire while breaking down biomass, lowering oxygen and harming aerobic animals. Temperature, sewage, flow or toxins could contribute; sample tributaries over time and compare controlled/less-affected sites. Use systematic transects with random quadrats/kick samples, standard effort, repeats, abiotic measurements and means/spread at multiple distances. They are oxygen sensitive, so decline supports poor quality, but life cycle, season and habitat also affect abundance. Decomposers recycle mineral ions, but excessive organic matter raises respiration and can deplete oxygen faster than it is replaced. If applied to 11 mg dm⁻³, 45% remains: about 5.0 mg dm⁻³; improvement is substantial but does not restore the 3 mg dm⁻³ baseline. It improves water, habitat and flood storage but removes farmland; compare ecosystem-service value, yield loss and alternative buffer strips. Reduce fertiliser runoff, add buffer strips/wetland, monitor nitrate/oxygen/biodiversity across seasons, and adjust measures using replicated trend data.
